opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those ideas I keep coming back to, partly because it cuts against a lot of intuitions people have about what neural networks can and can't do.

Cryptographic hash functions are designed to be maximally chaotic. Flip one bit of the input and roughly half the output bits flip. There's no smooth structure, no gradient to follow, nothing a function approximator should be able to latch onto. So the standard assumption is that deep learning is useless here. These functions are essentially the adversarial worst case for interpolation.

What interests me is that "worst case on average" isn't the same as "no exploitable structure anywhere." Neural nets have repeatedly surprised us by finding regularities we didn't know were there. Protein folding looked combinatorially hopeless, and it turned out there was a lot of learnable structure in the distribution of proteins that actually exist. So I wonder whether there are similar pockets in cryptographic primitives. Maybe not breaking SHA-256 outright, but reduced-round versions, or specific input distributions, or partial information about certain output bits that's slightly better than chance.

And "slightly better than chance" matters a lot in crypto. A tiny statistical bias, compounded over many samples, is basically what classical differential and linear cryptanalysis is. Humans found those attacks by hand, with a lot of clever reasoning. Could a learned system search that space of distinguishers more broadly than human cryptanalysts can? There's been some early work on neural distinguishers for reduced-round ciphers like Speck that did surprisingly well, which I find very suggestive.

There's also a more philosophical angle. If you could build a fast learned approximation to something like a hash, even an imperfect one, it would tell you something deep about the relationship between computational hardness and learnability. Much of complexity theory rests on the assumption that certain functions are hard to invert or predict. If learned systems start eroding that at the margins, either our hardness assumptions are weaker in practice than we thought, or we learn something interesting about which problems are hard for gradient descent specifically versus hard in general.

And practically, if you can approximate expensive functions cheaply, that's useful well beyond breaking things. Think proof-of-work, simulation, or any situation where you need to call an expensive deterministic function billions of times. Even a fast approximate oracle you can use to prune a search could be a big deal.

To be clear, I'm not predicting someone trains a transformer that cracks SHA-256 next year. I'd bet heavily against that. But I think the community has been too confident that this area is off limits to learning, and testing that boundary is exactly where interesting surprises tend to come from.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing that fascinates me is that cryptographic hashes are, almost by design, the functions that are supposed to be impossible to approximate. The whole point of SHA-256 is that it's maximally sensitive to its inputs. You flip one bit and the output looks totally uncorrelated. There's no smooth structure, no gradient to follow. It's the exact opposite of the kind of function neural networks are good at learning.

And yet I think it's a really useful thought experiment, because it forces you to ask: what does "approximation" even mean for a function like that? If you ask a model to predict the first few bits of a hash, you expect it to do no better than chance. That's a security property. But the interesting cases are the ones that sit in between. Things like locality-sensitive hashing, where you actually want similar inputs to collide, and the function is deliberately smooth in some metric. That's basically what an embedding model is. So there's this spectrum from "perfectly unlearnable" to "perfectly learnable," and a lot of practical systems live somewhere in the middle without anyone having thought carefully about where.

The other thing I find interesting is the compute angle. A hash is cheap to compute exactly, so why would you ever want a fast approximation? And the answer is usually that you're not approximating the hash, you're approximating some computation that uses the hash as a subroutine. Like a lookup, or a membership check, or a verification step. Bloom filters are a classic example. You're trading a little bit of error for a huge win in memory and speed. And I think as we put models into more and more systems, we're going to see a lot of places where people say, "I don't need the exact answer, I need the right answer ninety-nine percent of the time and I need it in one forward pass."

Where it gets a little philosophically spicy is when you point the question at the model itself. A transformer is a big, deterministic function. In principle you could think of it as a very expensive hash of its input. And people are already asking, can you approximate that hash with a smaller network? That's distillation. So in some sense the entire field of model compression is the question of which parts of this big function have structure that can be learned cheaply and which parts are effectively random. I don't think we have a good theory of that yet, and the cryptography framing is one of the few places where people have actually proven hardness results about it. So I keep coming back to it as a source of intuition, even if I don't expect anyone to break SHA with a neural net.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is whether a computation that’s hard to do exactly might still have a useful approximation. In a lot of machine learning, that’s the whole game: you replace an expensive computation with something cheap that’s good enough.

Cryptography is a particularly interesting place to test that intuition because it’s designed to resist shortcuts. With a cryptographic hash, getting an output that’s almost right generally doesn’t help you. A small change in the input should scramble the output, and being one bit off still means you have the wrong hash.

But you could ask a different question: can a learned model predict some property of the result, or narrow the search space, more cheaply than doing the full computation? That wouldn’t necessarily break the system, but it could reveal structure we didn’t expect. I don’t know that such a shortcut exists for a strong hash. The interesting thing is the boundary—where does learning give you a useful approximation, and where do you really have to do the work?

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is whether there are computations that are fundamentally hard to approximate, even with learning. In a lot of domains, we discover that you don’t actually have to execute the whole algorithm. You can learn a shortcut that gets you close enough. Cryptography is deliberately trying to prevent that.

Take a hash function. You can train a neural network to predict its output, but knowing almost all the input bits shouldn’t let you predict the output much better than chance. And getting an output that’s close in Hamming distance is usually useless. You need the exact bits.

But there’s a subtle distinction between predicting the answer and finding a faster way to compute it. A function could have no useful statistical approximation and still have some computational shortcut we haven’t discovered. So I’m curious about whether learning systems can find those shortcuts—or whether cryptographic problems give us a particularly clean example of where learning runs into a wall.
